source_refs.note: Chapter 29 exercise (PDF 199-201), solved: 6 MCQs keyed (no key is printed), 4 short, 2 constructed-response and 3 descriptive questions with model answers; spectra described in words. MCQ V, MCQ VI and Short Q2(d) carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt:
I) Which of the following compounds could produce the IR spectrum shown below?
(IR spectrum printed: transmittance (%) from 0 to 100 against wavenumber (cm⁻¹) from 4000 to 500. A very broad, deep band centred near 3400 cm⁻¹; a pair of sharp bands near 2950–2900 cm⁻¹ marked X; a very strong, sharp band near 1710 cm⁻¹ marked Y; several bands below 1500 cm⁻¹.)
blocks.explanation:
The spectrum shows two groups (Table 29.2):
Broad band near 3400 cm⁻¹ (3200–3600): O–H of an alcohol (hydroxy), not the very broad 2500–3300 band of a carboxylic acid.
Strong, sharp band near 1710 cm⁻¹ (1670–1740): C=O of a carbonyl group.
Only 4-hydroxybutanone, HOCH₂CH₂COCH₃, has both an alcohol O–H and a C=O. Pentan-1-ol and 2-hydroxybut-1-ene have no C=O; propanoic acid would give the broader 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ O–H band.

blocks.prompt: II) What is the wavelength range of the UV spectrum?
blocks.explanation: UV-Vis spectroscopy uses wavelengths from 200 to 800 nm to study changes in electronic energy levels (29.4).

blocks.prompt: III) The λ of σ to σ* transitions lies in the
blocks.explanation: σ bonding orbitals are the lowest in energy and σ* the highest, so σ→σ* needs the most energy, i.e. the shortest wavelength. This lies in the UV region (in fact below 200 nm, the far UV, so ordinary UV-Vis instruments do not record it).

blocks.prompt: IV) The types of transitions possible in UV-visible region for a compound with molecular formula C₂H₄ are:
blocks.explanation: C₂H₄ is ethene, CH₂=CH₂: it has σ and π electrons but no non-bonding (n) electrons, so n→π* and n→σ* are impossible. σ→σ* needs too much energy (below 200 nm). The transition in the UV-visible range is π→π*.

blocks.prompt: V) What is index of hydrogen deficiency of C₈H₈?
blocks.explanation:
Saturated alkane with 8 C: C₈H₁₈ (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂)
Hydrogens missing = 18 − 8 = 10
IHD = 10 / 2 = 5
No option gives 5 (see the Book correction). (d) 4 is keyed as the closest; it would be right for C₈H₁₀.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: No option is correct: C₈H₈ (e.g. styrene, a benzene ring plus one C=C) has IHD = (18 − 8)/2 = 5. Option (d) 4 is keyed as the nearest; it would be correct for C₈H₁₀ (e.g. ethylbenzene).

blocks.prompt: VI) Which of the following statements about the mass spectrum of CH₃Cl is correct?

options.text: There is one peak for the molecular ion with an m/e value of 45.
There is one peak for the molecular ion with an m/e value of 52.
The last two peaks have abundances in the ratio 1:1 and occur at m/e values of 50 and 52.
The last two peaks are of equal size and occur at m/e values of 50 and 52.

blocks.explanation:
CH₃³⁵Cl: 12 + 3 + 35 = 50 (M⁺ peak)
CH₃³⁷Cl: 12 + 3 + 37 = 52 ([M+2] peak)
So there are two molecular ion peaks, at 50 and 52, in the ratio 3:1 (³⁵Cl is three times as abundant as ³⁷Cl). Options (c) and (d) give the right m/e values but a 1:1 ratio, which belongs to bromine; see the Book correction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: No option is fully correct: the two molecular ion peaks of CH₃Cl at m/e 50 and 52 are in the ratio 3:1, not 1:1. Options (c) and (d) say the same thing (1:1 = equal size). Option (c) is keyed as the intended answer, read with the ratio 3:1.

blocks.prompt:
a) Bromobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, can be reacted with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide to prepare butan-1-ol.
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
Butan-1-ol produced can be analysed by mass spectrometry.
i. Predict the formula of fragment ion which is produced to m/e value of 17.
ii. Predict two other fragment ions that you would expect to see in the mass spectrum of butan-1-ol and state the m/e value of each ion.
blocks.explanation:
i. m/e 17 = OH⁺ (16 + 1).
ii. Breaking C–C bonds gives, e.g., C₂H₅⁺ (m/e 29) and C₃H₇⁺ (m/e 43); others are CH₃⁺ (15), CH₂OH⁺ (31) and C₄H₉⁺ (57). The molecular ion C₄H₉OH⁺ is at m/e 74.

blocks.prompt:
b) Identify the functional groups responsible for the peaks labelled X and Y.
(IR spectrum printed: transmittance (%) from 0 to 100 against wavenumber (cm⁻¹) from 4000 to 500. A very broad, deep band centred near 3400 cm⁻¹; a pair of sharp bands near 2950–2900 cm⁻¹ marked X; a very strong, sharp band near 1710 cm⁻¹ marked Y; several bands below 1500 cm⁻¹.)
blocks.explanation:
X (about 2950–2900 cm⁻¹, range 2850–2950): C–H bonds of an alkyl (sp³) group.
Y (about 1710 cm⁻¹, strong and sharp, range 1670–1740): C=O of a carbonyl group (ketone).
(The broad band near 3400 cm⁻¹ is an alcohol O–H.)

blocks.prompt:
c) Explain how the two isomers shown in the diagram can be distinguished using IR spectroscopy.
(Diagram: A is cyclopentanone, a five-membered ring with a C=O group; B is a five-membered ring with an OH group at the top carbon and a C=C double bond in the ring at the bottom, i.e. cyclopent-3-en-1-ol. Both are C₅H₈O.)
blocks.explanation:
A (ketone) gives a strong, sharp C=O band at 1670–1740 cm⁻¹ and no O–H band.
B (alcohol with C=C) gives a broad O–H band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and a C=C band at 1500–1680 cm⁻¹, but no C=O band near 1700 cm⁻¹.

blocks.prompt:
d) The molecular formulas of but-1-ene and but-1,4-diene are given below:
but-1-ene: C₄H₈   but-1,3-diene: C₄H₆
i. Fine out the IHD for both of these compounds.
ii. Compare the UV absorption spectrum of but-1-ene to that of but-1,3-diene by stating the difference in their λₘₐₓ qualitatively.
blocks.explanation:
i. Saturated C₄: C₄H₁₀.
but-1-ene C₄H₈: IHD = (10 − 8)/2 = 1 (one C=C)
buta-1,3-diene C₄H₆: IHD = (10 − 6)/2 = 2 (two C=C)
ii. Buta-1,3-diene has two conjugated C=C bonds, so the π→π* gap is smaller and its λₘₐₓ is longer (217 nm). But-1-ene has one isolated C=C, a larger gap and a shorter λₘₐₓ (below about 200 nm).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The stem prints “but-1,4-diene”, but the formula line names but-1,3-diene, C₄H₆; a four-carbon chain cannot have double bonds at 1 and 4 (the correct name is buta-1,3-diene). Part i prints “Fine out”, meaning “Find out”.

blocks.prompt: a) Compound X is an atmospheric pollutant emitted from fuel combustion of petrol and diesel vehicles. Compound X is a potent human carcinogen. Analysis of compound X showed the following percentage composition by mass: C, 88.89% and H, 11.1%. Mass spectrometry showed a molecular ion peak at m/e = 54. Compound X reacts with H₂ in the presence of a nickel catalyst in a 1 : 2 molar ratio. Analyse and interpret this information to determine a possible structure for compound X. Show all your working.
blocks.explanation:
Given: C = 88.89 %, H = 11.1 %, M⁺ at m/e 54 (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
1. Moles in 100 g:
C: 88.89 / 12 = 7.41 mol
H: 11.1 / 1 = 11.1 mol
2. Ratio: 7.41 / 7.41 = 1 ; 11.1 / 7.41 = 1.50
× 2 → C : H = 2 : 3, empirical formula C₂H₃ (mass 27)
3. n = 54 / 27 = 2, molecular formula C₄H₆
4. IHD = (10 − 6)/2 = 2
5. 1 mol X adds 2 mol H₂, so both degrees of unsaturation are π bonds (no ring): two C=C or one C≡C.
6. A petrol/diesel exhaust pollutant and carcinogen with formula C₄H₆ and two C=C: buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂.
CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ + 2H₂ → (Ni) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃

blocks.prompt:
b) How will you differentiate between the following using the UV visible spectroscopy.
(Structures printed: i) a cyclohexene ring whose ring C=C starts at the carbon that carries a –CH=CH–CH=CH₂ side chain, so three C=C bonds are conjugated; ii) a cyclohexane (saturated) ring carrying the same –CH=CH–CH=CH₂ side chain, so only two C=C bonds are conjugated.)
blocks.explanation:
Both absorb by π→π* transitions, but they differ in conjugation:
(i) has three conjugated C=C bonds (ring C=C plus the diene side chain), so its energy gap is smaller and its λₘₐₓ is longer.
(ii) has only two conjugated C=C bonds (the ring is saturated), so its λₘₐₓ is shorter, close to that of a simple diene.
Each extra conjugated C=C raises λₘₐₓ by roughly 30–40 nm, so (i) absorbs at a clearly longer wavelength than (ii).

blocks.prompt: Q4. Describe various possible electronic transitions in a compound having sigma, pi bonds, and non-bonding electrons.
blocks.explanation:
A compound can have three types of electrons: σ electrons (single bonds), π electrons (multiple bonds, unsaturated compounds) and n electrons (lone pairs, e.g. on O, N, halogens).
Orbital energies: σ (bonding) < π (bonding) < n (non-bonding) < π* (anti-bonding) < σ* (anti-bonding). The bonding and non-bonding orbitals are filled; π* and σ* are normally empty.
When UV-Vis light of the right energy is absorbed, an electron jumps from a filled orbital to an empty anti-bonding orbital:
1. σ→σ*: largest energy gap, shortest wavelength (below 200 nm); occurs in all compounds, e.g. alkanes.
2. n→σ*: lone-pair electron to σ*; e.g. alcohols, amines, alkyl halides.
3. π→π*: in compounds with C=C, C=O, C≡C; e.g. buta-1,3-diene, λₘₐₓ 217 nm. Conjugation lowers the gap and increases λₘₐₓ (butadiene 217, hexatriene 257, octatetraene 290 nm).
4. n→π*: smallest energy gap, longest wavelength; in compounds with a lone pair next to a π bond, e.g. C=O in aldehydes and ketones.
(σ→π* and π→σ* are also possible but less important.)
Energy order: σ→σ* > n→σ* > π→π* > n→π*.
The important transitions in the 200–800 nm range are π→π*, n→π* and n→σ*. Each transition absorbs light of a definite wavelength, and the wavelength of maximum absorption is λₘₐₓ.

blocks.prompt: Q5. Explain two types of atomic spectrum.
blocks.explanation:
Atomic spectra arise when electrons of atoms move between discrete energy levels; they show that atomic energy is quantized.
1. Emission spectrum: produced by heating a low-pressure gas. Heat excites electrons to higher levels; when they fall back to lower levels they emit photons of definite energy, E = hν. Each transition gives one wavelength, seen as a bright coloured line on a black background. E.g. hydrogen gives lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm (transitions from n = 6, 5, 4, 3 down to n = 2).
2. Absorption spectrum: produced by passing white light through a cool, low-pressure gas. Only photons with exactly the energy needed to excite electrons from the ground state are absorbed; these wavelengths appear as dark lines on a continuous coloured background.
The dark lines of the absorption spectrum are at the same wavelengths as the bright lines of the emission spectrum of the same element; one is like a photographic negative of the other. Each element has its own unique pattern of lines (a fingerprint), so atomic spectra identify elements, e.g. sodium's yellow line at 589 nm.

rows: Produced by heating a low-pressure gas
Produced by passing white light through a cool, low-pressure gas
Excited electrons fall to lower levels and emit photons
Ground-state electrons absorb photons and rise to higher levels
Bright coloured lines on a black background
Dark lines on a continuous coloured background
Lines at the same wavelengths as the absorption lines
Like a photographic negative of the emission spectrum

blocks.prompt: Q6. How mass spectrometry is used to determine the isotopic mass and average atomic masses of elements? Explain giving an example.
blocks.explanation:
In a mass spectrometer, atoms of the sample are bombarded with high-energy electrons; each atom loses an electron and forms a positive ion. The ions are separated and detected according to their mass-to-charge ratio, and the spectrum is recorded as % abundance against m/e.
Isotopic mass: each isotope of an element gives a separate peak; since the charge is +1, the m/e value of the peak is the mass of that isotope.
Relative abundance: the height of each peak shows the proportion (relative abundance) of that isotope in the natural mixture.
Average (relative) atomic mass is then calculated:
Aᵣ = Σ (isotopic mass × % abundance) / 100
Example, boron: the spectrum shows peaks at m/e 10 (19.9 %) and m/e 11 (80.1 %).
Aᵣ = [(10 × 19.9) + (11 × 80.1)] / 100
Aᵣ = (199 + 881.1) / 100 = 1080.1 / 100
Aᵣ = 10.80
Similarly, chlorine (³⁵Cl 75 %, ³⁷Cl 25 %): Aᵣ = [(35 × 75) + (37 × 25)] / 100 = 35.5
